newsitem.title: USA: Senators hear U.S. refuge bid by Swiss bank guard.
newsitem.headline: Senators hear U.S. refuge bid by Swiss bank guard.

text.p: The young Swiss security guard who tried to stop Nazi-era bank records from being shredded said on Tuesday he is being threatened, harassed and hounded at home and asked for refuge in the United States.

"I fear for the safety of my wife and two children. We are afraid," Christoph Meili, 29, told a Senate Immigration subcommittee which is considering a special bill that would swiftly grant his family permanent U.S. residency. They would not qualify under routine immigration procedures.

The panel did not take any immediate action, but many senators have lavished praise on Meili, who was a student by day and security guard by night at the Union Bank of Switzerland when he stumbled on the carts of Holocaust-era documents waiting for the shredder.

Switzerland has said it is investigating its bank dealings with the Nazis and trying to determine what happened to the assets of Jews and other victims of the Holocaust. Three weeks before the bank incident, Switzerland enacted a law making it illegal to destroy documents related to that probe.
"I am a very simple man with a modest life style," Meili said through an interpreter. "I did not think of becoming a hero."
He said he now receives hate mail, death threats, even threats to kidnap and kill his two children, Miriam, four, and David, two.
"My family's life has been turned into a living hell," he said. He was fired, and has been called a traitor, criminal and "agent" of the Jews, he said.

He accused Swiss banks, police and government authorities of hoping to keep hidden the nation's past dealings with Nazis, and accused authorities of failing to do anything with the documents he turned over in January.
"There are certain powers in Switzerland who do not want to see the Swiss banks and government exposed for what they did in the Holocaust," he said.

New York Republican Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, who has been central in bringing the Nazi gold scandal to public attention, urged the Senate to pass the immigration bill. "Human decency cries out for the world to protect him," he said.
Edgar Bronfman, president of the Seagram company and chairman of the World Jewish Congress, has offered Meili a job.
